issues.legal_issue: An appellate court should not disturb a trial court’s discretionary decision on specific performance unless that discretion was exercised perversely, arbitrarily, or contrary to judicial principles.
material_facts: The trial court considered the pleadings and evidence, found that a valid sale agreement had been executed and advance consideration paid, and decreed specific performance.
The High Court reversed the decree, relying in part on the purchaser’s complaints to the police and its view that the seller had signed under pressure.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court had not approached the evidence in the proper perspective and had committed a serious error in its assessment.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have displaced the trial court’s exercise of discretion on the grounds it relied on; its judgment was set aside and the trial court’s decree restored, subject to a modification of the consideration.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, specific performance is discretionary, but the discretion is judicial rather than arbitrary and must follow sound legal and equitable principles. As stated in Rooke’s Case (1597) 5 Co. Rep. 99 and Attorney General v. Wheat (1759) 1 Eden 177, judicial discretion is governed by rules of law and equity. An appellate court normally should not interfere with the trial court’s exercise of discretion unless it was perverse, arbitrary, or contrary to judicial principles, and should not refuse relief on extraneous or merely sympathetic considerations.

predicates.specific_performance_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a decree granting or refusing specific performance of a contract.
predicates.trial_court_exercised_discretion: The trial court considered the evidence and exercised its discretion in deciding whether to grant specific performance.
predicates.trial_discretion_perverse_arbitrary_or_a: The trial court exercised its discretion perversely, arbitrarily, or contrary to judicial principles.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns specific performance and the trial court exercised its discretion without perversity, arbitrariness, or departure from judicial principles, the appellate court should not interfere with that exercise.

issues.legal_issue: Specific performance is warranted when a valid sale agreement is proved and the purchaser establishes continued readiness and willingness to perform, unless a proper equitable ground justifies refusing relief.
material_facts: The trial court found that the seller had signed the sale agreement and admitted in cross-examination that he had read and signed the papers.
A subsequent letter signed by the seller acknowledged the agreement and receipt of the advance consideration.
The purchaser had paid or arranged substantial amounts toward the transaction and arranged funds for the balance consideration and registration charges.
The purchaser asserted that he remained ready and willing to perform, and the trial court granted specific performance after considering the evidence.

The seller alleged that the agreement was signed under pressure and was intended only to secure a loan; the Supreme Court rejected the High Court’s conclusion that the agreement was executed without free mind and volition.
issues.conclusion: The agreement was validly proved, and the purchaser’s claim for specific performance was allowed, subject to the condition that he pay an increased total consideration.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires a plaintiff seeking specific performance to prove continued readiness and willingness to perform the essential terms of the contract from the contract date through the hearing. Under Section 20, once a valid agreement and the requirements for relief are established, the court should exercise its discretion in favour of specific performance unless a proper equitable consideration justifies otherwise.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.sale_agreement_validly_proved: The purchaser proves that the parties entered into a valid sale agreement.
predicates.purchaser_continuously_ready_and_willing: The purchaser demonstrates continued readiness and willingness to perform the purchaser’s contractual obligations.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance suit, proof of a valid sale agreement and the purchaser’s continued readiness and willingness supports granting relief unless a proper equitable ground justifies refusal.

issues.legal_issue: A rise in property value during litigation does not, by itself, justify refusing specific performance.
material_facts: The seller argued that the agreed price was low and that the property’s value had increased substantially during the litigation.
The Supreme Court regarded the increase in price as a normal change of circumstances and held that it was not, by itself, hardship requiring refusal of specific performance.
issues.conclusion: The increase in property value during the litigation did not justify reversing the specific-performance decree on its own.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, the court exercises equitable discretion by considering the totality of the circumstances. Nirmala Anand v. Advent Corporation (P) Ltd., (2002) 8 SCC 146, holds that phenomenal appreciation during litigation ordinarily does not alone defeat specific performance, though it may be considered alongside other circumstances when balancing the equities.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.property_value_increased_during_litigati: The value of the property increased while the specific-performance dispute was being litigated.
predicates.increase_is_the_only_ground_for_refusal: The asserted ground for refusing specific performance is the increase in the property’s value, without an additional circumstance justifying refusal.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance suit, an increase in property value during litigation, when it is the only asserted ground for refusal, does not justify refusing the requested relief.

issues.legal_issue: A court granting specific performance may require additional consideration to balance the equities when circumstances, including a substantial increase in property value, warrant that condition.
material_facts: The agreement had been made several years before the Supreme Court’s decision, and the property’s value had increased substantially in the meantime.
The seller relied on the increase in value as a hardship, while the Court concluded that the increase alone did not warrant refusing specific performance.
Considering the elapsed time, the scale of the increase, and the circumstances as a whole, the Court required a higher total consideration as a condition of completing the sale.
issues.conclusion: The specific-performance decree was restored on condition that the purchaser pay increased consideration, less the amount already paid, and the seller execute a registered sale deed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 permits the court to impose a reasonable condition when granting specific performance. Nirmala Anand v. Advent Corporation (P) Ltd., (2002) 8 SCC 146, recognizes that an additional payment may be required to balance the equities, having regard to the totality of the circumstances, including who defaulted, whether a party seeks an undue advantage, and the hardship caused.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.substantial_property_value_increase: The property’s value has increased substantially since the contract was made.
predicates.court_finds_equities_require_compensatio: The court finds, after considering the circumstances as a whole, that compensation is appropriate to balance the equities.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance suit, where property value has increased substantially and the circumstances warrant compensation, the court may require additional compensation as a condition of relief.
